Hi Chloe,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — the team at FinAsset is excited to move forward with a 6-week pilot. Before we lock dates, procurement asked for clarity on how your credits/packaging work. Two quick asks: 

1) For the pilot workload below, would you recommend a slab (reserved) credit band or burst credits (on-demand)? Which tends to be more cost-effective for early pilots?
2) Any recommended quantization/precision guidance for a small production pilot? We care about response quality over millisecond-level latency, but want obvious cost wins if possible.

Pilot workload (rough):
- Peak concurrency: ~150 concurrent sessions (mostly short prompts)
- Avg prompt length: 120 tokens in, 220 tokens out
- Typical seq length distribution: 90% < 512 tokens, 10% up to 1,024 tokens
- Expected daily throughput: ~300k tokens/day

I've attached a small traffic sample (pilot-traffic-sample.csv) to give you realistic token distribution. Procurement wants an informal pricing sketch so they can greenlight the PO.

Appreciate the quick turnaround — copying procurement.

From: Chloe Martin <chloe_martin@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Piloting Redwood Optimize — credit model question

Maya — thanks for the sample and the clear breakdown. High level up front: both slab and burst can make sense for a pilot, but the economics and operational tradeoffs differ. Quick summary and an actionable plan below.

Summary (short):
- Slab (reserved): best when you can commit to a predictable baseline (e.g., sustained throughput). Gives a lower per-token effective cost during utilization and priority capacity. However, it requires committing credits up front.
- Burst (on-demand): no upfront commit; you pay list rates for overage. Simpler procurement for pilots but higher unit cost if steady traffic materializes.

Given your sample (300k tokens/day, peaks at 150 concurrent), my short recommendation: start the pilot on a small slab that covers ~60% of expected steady-state throughput + burstable headroom. That gives predictable costs for your baseline and keeps the ability to spike.

Why this mix?
- The slab covers the high-utilization window and lets us offer a modest discount immediately.
- Leaving burst capacity avoids throttling during unexpected spikes and reduces risk during traffic variability.

Quantization and KV caching guidance:
- Quantization: For a pilot prioritized on quality, start with int8 (8-bit) quantization for non-critical endpoints and float16 for your most sensitive prompts. We often recommend an AB test: int8 vs f16 on a representative eval set to measure quality delta.
- KV cache: prefix/KV caching yields the biggest per-token savings when you have short repeated contexts (e.g., system prompts, few-shot examples). For your workload, a ttl-based cache with 60–300s TTLs tends to capture session-level repetition while avoiding stale state.

Proposed mutual action plan (MAP):
1) Week 0: Agree SLAs/metrics and sign a short (6-week) pilot order — we can do a small slab credit commit of 500k tokens/day equivalent for the pilot duration.
2) Week 1: Onboarding + deploy model variants: int8 and f16. Baseline traffic routed 60/40 slab/burst.
3) Week 2–4: Collect quality metrics (SFT logs + eval set) and runtime telemetry (p50/p95 latencies, cache hit rate).
4) Week 5–6: Review results; if quality delta is acceptable, propose a production commit with tiered slab pricing (higher discount at larger commit bands).

I've attached a one-pager that summarizes slab vs burst and a rough cost sketch (redwood-slab-vs-burst-onepager.pdf). If it helps, we can produce a line-item cost model for procurement showing expected token spend and effective unit price under the 60/40 scenario.

Would you be available for a 30-minute sync tomorrow to run through the numbers? If procurement prefers, we can also provide a draft PO template and a short DocuSign flow.

Cheers,
Chloe Martin
Senior Sales Manager, Cloud & Enterprise
Redwood Inference

Adding a couple of technical/contract notes from the inference side that often matter for pilots: 

Technical nuance:
- Model choice: If FinAsset values quality, pick the f16 variant for any customer-facing prompts where hallucination risk is unacceptable; that said, int8 is often within noise for many tasks and gives ~1.6x–2.2x token cost reduction depending on the model family.
- KV cache configuration: Recommend an adaptive TTL that increases hit probability during session bursts. We can instrument a short experiment (change TTL from 60s -> 300s) and measure hit-rate lift; expect 15–35% token savings in the kind of short-session workload you shared.
- Batching: Keep batch windows tight for latency-sensitive routes (we'll set batching to 20–50ms) and allow larger batch sizes for backend generation jobs. This dual-config reduces unit cost while protecting p95 latency.

Commercial suggestion (practical):
- Pilot credit split: 60% slab (prepaid credit applied to baseline), 40% burst (pay-as-you-go at list).
- Pilot discount structure: 10% off list for the slab portion during a 6-week pilot + an additional 5% rebate post-pilot if baseline utilization exceeds 70% of the slab for 10 consecutive days.
- If FinAsset signs a 6–12 month commit post-pilot, we can convert pilot slab credits into committed capacity at a deeper discount (scoped by monthly token commit bands).

If helpful I can sketch the numerical model with your CSV and run a sensitivity table (slab size vs effective cost per token). Chloe — happy to take point on that modeling if you want.

—Vanessa

Redwood Inference
